column9: What is the most accurate definition of cancer?
column14: A disease of uncontrolled cell growth and division
column15: A viral infection that makes cells change shape
column16: A total lack of cell division in an organ
column17: The natural death of cells that are no longer needed
column28: Cancer is a disease in which cells grow and divide out of control. The natural death of unneeded cells is apoptosis, which actually protects against cancer.
column29: Think about what goes wrong with the cell cycle in cancer.

column9: A mass of cells that stays in its original location and does not spread is called a:
column14: Malignant tumor
column15: Carcinogen
column16: Metastatic growth
column17: Benign tumor
column28: A benign tumor stays in one place and does not spread. A malignant tumor is cancerous and can invade and spread. A carcinogen is something that causes cancer.
column29: A carcinogen causes cancer. Of the other choices, which one describes a tumor that is not cancer?

column9: What happens during metastasis?
column14: Damaged cells destroy themselves by programmed cell death
column15: Cancer cells break away and form tumors in new places
column16: The cell cycle slows and the tumor shrinks
column17: A benign tumor is removed from the body by surgery
column28: Metastasis is when cancer cells break off a malignant tumor, travel through the blood or lymph, and start new tumors in other parts of the body. Programmed cell death is apoptosis, and removing a benign tumor is surgery, not spreading.
column29: Meta- means change or beyond. The cancer moves beyond where it started.

column9: Substances or energy that can cause cancer by damaging a cell's DNA are called:
column14: Enzymes
column15: Hormones
column16: Carcinogens
column17: Antioxidants
column28: Carcinogens, like tobacco smoke and UV radiation, damage DNA and cause mutations that can lead to cancer. Enzymes speed up reactions, hormones are chemical messengers, and antioxidants help protect cells.
column29: Enzymes speed up reactions and hormones carry messages. Which word means 'cancer-causing'?

column9: What is apoptosis?
column14: Programmed death of damaged or unneeded cells
column15: The stage of mitosis where chromosomes line up
column16: The rapid, nonstop division of cancer cells
column17: A tumor growing its own new blood supply
column28: Apoptosis is programmed cell death: a cell destroys itself when it is damaged or no longer needed. It is one of the body's protections against cancer. Chromosomes lining up is metaphase.
column29: The word comes from Greek: apo- means 'away' and -ptosis means 'falling,' like leaves falling from a tree in autumn.

column9: A cancerous tumor that can invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body is called ___.
column28: Malignant tumors are cancerous: they invade nearby tissue and can metastasize. Benign tumors stay in one place.
column29: There are two kinds of tumors. This is the kind that is cancer and can spread.

column9: In cancer, cells keep dividing even when the body does not need new cells.
column28: True. Cancer is uncontrolled cell division: cancer cells keep dividing when they should stop, because the controls on their cell cycle are broken.
column29: Is cancer a problem with cells dividing too little or too much?

column9: All tumors are cancerous and dangerous.
column28: False. Benign tumors are not cancer: they stay in one place and don't spread. Only malignant tumors are cancerous.
column29: There are two kinds of tumors. Are both cancer?

column9: A person cannot do anything to reduce their risk of developing cancer.
column28: False. Some things that cause cancer can be avoided, like tobacco smoke and too much sun, and healthy habits lower the risk too. Regular checkups don't prevent cancer, but they help catch it early, when it is easier to treat.
column29: Think of carcinogens. Can a person choose to avoid some of them?

column9: Match each term to its description.
column14: Proto-oncogene :: A normal gene that tells the cell when to divide
column15: Oncogene :: A mutated version of a gene that tells the cell to divide
column16: Tumor suppressor gene :: A gene that slows or stops the cell cycle when something is wrong
column17: Checkpoint :: An inspection stop before the cell moves to the next phase
column28: A proto-oncogene is a normal gene that tells the cell to divide (the gas pedal). When it mutates, it becomes an oncogene (a stuck gas pedal). A tumor suppressor gene slows or stops the cycle when something is wrong (the brakes). A checkpoint is an inspection stop in the cell cycle.
column29: 'Proto-' means first or original. 'Suppress' means hold back.

column9: What is the main job of cell cycle checkpoints?
column14: To check the cell for problems before it moves on
column15: To copy all of the cell's DNA before it divides
column16: To push the cell through mitosis more quickly
column17: To destroy tumor cells after a tumor forms
column28: Checkpoints are inspection stops where the cell is checked, for example to make sure its DNA was copied correctly, before it moves on. DNA is copied in the S phase of interphase, not by a checkpoint, and checkpoints don't speed up mitosis or destroy tumors. Cancer cells ignore these checks.
column29: Think of a quality-control inspector on an assembly line.

column9: Which of these is a carcinogen?
column14: Vitamin C in orange juice
column15: Clean, filtered drinking water
column16: UV rays from a tanning bed
column17: Oxygen in the air you breathe
column28: UV rays (from tanning beds or the sun) damage the DNA in skin cells and can cause skin cancer, so they are a carcinogen. The other choices don't damage DNA.
column29: Which choice can cause a sunburn and damage skin cells' DNA?

column9: Normal cells divide only when the body needs new cells, such as for growth or repair.
column28: True. Normal cells respond to signals and checkpoints: they divide for growth and repair, then stop when the job is done.
column29: Think about why your skin stops growing over a cut once it is healed.

column9: Cancer starts with a change in a cell's DNA. What is a change in DNA called?
column14: A mutation
column15: Mitosis
column16: Metastasis
column17: Meiosis
column28: A mutation is a change in the DNA. Mutations in the genes that control the cell cycle can lead to cancer. Mitosis and meiosis are kinds of cell division, and metastasis is cancer spreading.
column29: Two of the choices are types of cell division, and one describes cancer spreading. Which one describes a change?

column9: What is a tumor?
column14: A group of cells that died by apoptosis
column15: A virus that infects and kills body cells
column16: A mass of extra cells from uncontrolled division
column17: A gene that controls when a cell divides
column28: A tumor is a lump or mass of extra cells that forms when cells divide out of control. It can be benign (stays put) or malignant (cancerous and can spread).
column29: What builds up when cells keep dividing and don't stop?

column9: In the car analogy, proto-oncogenes are the gas pedal and tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. What happens when a proto-oncogene mutates into an oncogene (the gas pedal gets stuck)?
column14: The cell slows down and stops dividing
column15: The cell goes through apoptosis right away
column16: The cell switches from mitosis to meiosis
column17: The cell keeps dividing when it shouldn't
column28: An oncogene is a stuck gas pedal: it keeps sending the 'divide' signal all the time, so the cell divides when it shouldn't. That can lead to a tumor.
column29: What does a car do when the gas pedal is stuck down?

column9: In the car analogy, proto-oncogenes are the gas pedal and tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. What happens when a tumor suppressor gene is damaged (the brakes fail)?
column14: The cell divides more slowly than normal
column15: Nothing stops the cell, so it keeps dividing
column16: The cell repairs all of its own DNA mistakes
column17: The cell leaves the cycle and never divides again
column28: Tumor suppressor genes normally slow or stop the cell cycle when something is wrong. If they are damaged, the cell has no brakes and keeps dividing.
column29: What happens to a car going downhill with no brakes?

column9: How is a malignant tumor different from a benign tumor?
column14: Only malignant tumors are caused by mutations
column15: Malignant tumors can invade nearby tissues and spread
column16: Malignant tumors are always smaller than benign ones
column17: Benign tumors are made only of dead or dying cells
column28: Malignant tumors are cancer: they invade nearby tissue and can spread (metastasize). Benign tumors also come from uncontrolled division, but they stay in one place. Size does not decide which kind a tumor is.
column29: The difference is about staying put versus spreading.

column9: Which choices lower a person's risk of cancer? Select all that apply.
column14: Wearing sunscreen outdoors
column15: Using a tanning bed before prom
column16: Not smoking or vaping
column17: Using chewing tobacco or snuff
column18: Eating fruits and vegetables and exercising
column28: Sunscreen blocks UV rays, not smoking avoids the carcinogens in smoke, and a healthy diet with exercise lowers risk. Tanning beds give off UV rays, and chewing tobacco and snuff contain carcinogens too, so they raise the risk of mouth and throat cancer.
column29: Pick the choices that avoid carcinogens or keep the body healthy.

column9: Which of these are carcinogens? Select all that apply.
column14: Visible light from a desk lamp
column15: Tobacco smoke
column16: UV rays from the sun
column17: Cold winter air
column28: Tobacco smoke, UV rays, and too much X-ray radiation can damage DNA and cause mutations, so they are carcinogens. Visible light from a lamp doesn't have enough energy to damage DNA the way UV rays do, and cold air doesn't damage DNA either.
column29: A carcinogen damages DNA. Which choices could do that?

column9: Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle, such as proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, can lead to cancer.
column28: True. These genes control when a cell divides. A mutation can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene (stuck gas pedal) or break a tumor suppressor gene (failed brakes), and the cell can start dividing out of control.
column29: Which genes act as the gas pedal and brakes of the cell cycle?

column9: A normal cell reaches a checkpoint, and its DNA is damaged. What should happen next?
column14: The cell divides faster to get rid of the damage
column15: The cell pauses for repair or goes through apoptosis
column16: The cell skips mitosis and turns into a tumor
column17: The cell copies the damaged DNA and keeps going
column28: At a checkpoint, a cell with damaged DNA is held back so the DNA can be repaired. If it can't be fixed, the cell destroys itself (apoptosis). Cancer cells skip this step and keep dividing with the damage.
column29: What would a quality-control inspector do with a broken part?

column9: How are cancer cells different from normal cells?
column14: They divide more slowly than normal cells
column15: They divide by meiosis instead of mitosis
column16: They stop dividing as soon as they touch
column17: They ignore checkpoints and keep dividing
column28: Cancer cells ignore the checkpoints and signals that tell normal cells to stop, so they keep dividing by mitosis. Normal cells, not cancer cells, stop dividing when they are crowded.
column29: Cancer is uncontrolled division. Which choice describes no control?

column9: In the Time for Mitosis lab, normal chicken stomach cells spend 540 minutes in interphase, but cancerous chicken stomach cells spend only 75 minutes. What does this show?
column14: Cancer cells spend more time growing before they divide
column15: Cancer cells skip interphase and go right to mitosis
column16: Cancer cells and normal cells divide at the same rate
column17: Cancer cells rush through interphase and divide more often
column28: Cancer cells spend far less time in interphase (75 vs 540 minutes), so they get back to mitosis much sooner and divide much more often. They still go through interphase, just quickly.
column29: Compare the two numbers. Which cell gets back to dividing sooner?

column9: Normal chicken stomach cells spend these times in each stage: interphase 540 min, prophase 60 min, metaphase 10 min, anaphase 3 min, telophase 12 min. How many minutes does one full cell cycle take?
column28: Add every stage: 540 + 60 + 10 + 3 + 12 = 625 minutes.
column29: Add the times for every stage listed.

column9: Cancerous chicken stomach cells spend these times in each stage: interphase 75 min, prophase 15 min, metaphase 2 min, anaphase 1 min, telophase 3 min. How many minutes does one full cell cycle take?
column28: Add every stage: 75 + 15 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 96 minutes. That is much shorter than a normal cell's cycle.
column29: Add the times for every stage listed.

column9: A classmate says, "Cancer only happens to old people." What is the best response?
column14: True: only older cells can pick up cancer-causing mutations
column15: Not true: risk rises with age, but young people can get it too
column16: True: young people's cells divide too slowly to form tumors
column17: Not true: cancer is equally common in people of every age
column28: Mutations build up over a lifetime, so cancer is more common in older people. But any cell can get a mutation, so children and teens can get cancer too.
column29: Mutations can happen at any age. What happens to them over many years?

column9: Put these steps in order to show how cancer can develop and spread.
column14: A carcinogen damages the DNA in a cell
column15: The cell ignores checkpoints and divides out of control
column16: A mass of extra cells forms a tumor
column17: New tumors form in other organs
column18: Cancer cells break away and enter the blood
column19: A mutation in a cell cycle gene is not repaired
column28: DNA damage → an unrepaired mutation in a cell cycle gene → uncontrolled division → a tumor → cells break away into the blood → new tumors elsewhere (metastasis).
column29: Think cause and effect: what must happen to a gene before a cell can ignore checkpoints, and what must form before cells can break away?

column9: Why is cancer called a disease of the cell cycle?
column14: Cancer cells leave the cell cycle and stop dividing
column15: Cancer is caught from another person's cells
column16: Cancer cells stay stuck in interphase and do not divide
column17: Its cells keep cycling and dividing without control
column28: Cancer happens when the controls on the cell cycle break, so cells keep cycling through interphase and mitosis over and over. It connects directly to mitosis (LT1): cancer is mitosis that won't stop.
column29: Connect it to mitosis. What happens to the cycle in a cancer cell?

column9: Match each cancer treatment to how it works.
column14: Surgery :: A doctor removes the tumor in an operation
column15: Chemotherapy :: Drugs travel through the blood and reach cells all over the body
column16: Radiation therapy :: High-energy rays aimed at the tumor damage its DNA
column28: Surgery cuts out the tumor. Chemotherapy uses drugs that travel through the blood, so they reach cancer cells anywhere in the body. Radiation therapy aims high-energy rays at the tumor to damage the cancer cells' DNA so they can't divide.
column29: One treatment uses an operation, one uses medicine, and one uses rays.

column9: A benign tumor can still cause health problems if it grows large enough to press on an organ, like the brain.
column28: True. Benign tumors don't spread, but they can still grow and press on nearby organs, nerves, or blood vessels. That is why doctors may still remove them.
column29: Benign means it does not spread. Can it still get big?

column9:
Normal skin cells and cancer cells were grown in two dishes and counted each day. Each dish has room for about 400 cells in a single layer.
Normal cells: Day 1: 100, Day 2: 200, Day 3: 400, Day 4: 400
Cancer cells: Day 1: 100, Day 2: 200, Day 3: 400, Day 4: 800
Which conclusion best fits the data?
column14: Cancer cells divided more slowly than the normal cells
column15: Both kinds of cells stopped dividing when the dish was full
column16: Normal cells stopped when crowded; cancer cells kept dividing
column17: Normal cells kept dividing, but the cancer cells stopped
column28: Both kinds of cells doubled each day at first. Once the dish was full (about 400 cells), the normal cells stopped dividing, but the cancer cells doubled again to 800 and piled on top of each other. Cancer cells don't respond to the signals to stop.
column29: Compare Day 3 to Day 4 for each kind of cell.

column9: Cancer cells often avoid apoptosis. How does this help a tumor grow?
column14: The cancer cells divide more slowly
column15: Damaged cells survive and keep dividing
column16: The damaged cells turn back into normal cells
column17: The tumor's cells die faster than they divide
column28: Apoptosis normally removes damaged cells. If cancer cells avoid it, damaged cells survive and keep dividing, so the tumor grows.
column29: Apoptosis is a self-destruct button. What happens if it doesn't work?

column9: Cancer that starts in the heart is very rare. One reason is that most heart muscle cells have left the cell cycle and stay in a resting stage where they no longer divide. This resting stage is called ___.
column20: G0|G 0|G-0|G zero|G-zero|Gzero|GO|G0 phase|G0 stage|gap 0|gap zero|G nought
column28: G0 is the resting stage outside the cell cycle. Cells in G0, like most heart muscle cells and nerve cells, don't divide. Cancer is uncontrolled cell division, so cancer rarely starts in tissues whose cells almost never divide. G0 is not part of interphase (G1, S, G2), where cells are getting ready to divide.
column29: Think back to the parts of the cell cycle. Where do cells go when they stop cycling, like most nerve cells?

column9: Which person has the highest risk of getting skin cancer?
column14: An office worker who wears sunscreen on weekends
column15: A lifeguard at an outdoor pool who skips sunscreen
column16: A student who spends most afternoons reading indoors
column17: A swimmer who trains only at an indoor pool all year
column28: Skin cancer is linked to UV rays. The lifeguard gets the most UV exposure with no protection, so their skin cells get the most DNA damage.
column29: Which carcinogen causes skin cancer, and who gets the most of it?

column9:
Chicken stomach cell times (minutes):
Normal: interphase 540, prophase 60, metaphase 10, anaphase 3, telophase 12
Cancerous: interphase 75, prophase 15, metaphase 2, anaphase 1, telophase 3
How many times faster does a cancerous cell finish one full cell cycle than a normal cell? Round to the nearest tenth.
column28: Normal total = 540 + 60 + 10 + 3 + 12 = 625 minutes. Cancer total = 75 + 15 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 96 minutes. Times faster = normal time ÷ cancer time = 625 ÷ 96 = 6.51, or about 6.5 times faster.
column29: Find the total time for each kind of cell first. Then divide the longer time by the shorter time.

column9: In the Time for Mitosis lab data, a normal chicken stomach cell spends 540 min in interphase, 60 min in prophase, 10 min in metaphase, 3 min in anaphase, and 12 min in telophase. What **percent** of its whole cell cycle is interphase?
column28: Total = 540 + 60 + 10 + 3 + 12 = 625 minutes. Percent = (540 ÷ 625) × 100 = 0.864 × 100 = 86.4%. Like most cells, it spends most of its life in interphase.
column29: Find the total time first. Then divide the interphase time by the total and multiply by 100.

column9: Cancerous chicken stomach cells spend 75 min in interphase, 15 min in prophase, 2 min in metaphase, 1 min in anaphase, and 3 min in telophase. If a cell never stops dividing, how many complete cell cycles can it finish in 24 hours (1,440 minutes)?
column28: One cycle = 75 + 15 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 96 minutes. Cycles = 1,440 ÷ 96 = 15 cycles. One cell doubling 15 times would make 2^{15} = 32,768 cells in a single day.
column29: Find how long one cycle takes. Then see how many of those fit into 1,440 minutes.

column9: People getting chemotherapy often lose their hair and feel sick to their stomach. What is the best explanation?
column14: The drugs make the hair and stomach cells turn into cancer cells
column15: The drugs collect mainly in the hair roots and stomach lining
column16: The drugs cause new tumors to grow in the hair roots and stomach
column17: The drugs hit all fast-dividing cells, like hair and stomach cells
column28: Chemotherapy works by killing cells that divide quickly. Cancer cells divide fast, but so do normal hair follicle cells and stomach lining cells, so they get hit too. That causes the side effects.
column29: Think about what chemotherapy targets. Which normal cells share that trait with cancer cells?

column9: You have two copies of most genes, one from each parent. A proto-oncogene usually causes trouble when just one copy mutates, but a tumor suppressor gene usually needs both copies damaged. Which car analogy explains this?
column14: One stuck gas pedal does nothing as long as the other pedal works
column15: One broken brake is enough to make the car speed out of control
column16: Both pedals must stick and both brakes must fail before the car speeds up
column17: One stuck gas pedal speeds the car up, but one good brake can still stop it
column28: An oncogene is a stuck gas pedal: one mutated copy sending 'go' all the time is enough to push the cell to divide. A tumor suppressor gene is a brake: as long as one copy still works, the cell can still stop. Both copies must fail before the brakes are gone. That rules out the choices where one stuck pedal does nothing, one broken brake is enough, or everything must fail at once.
column29: Which kind of mutation adds a 'go' signal, and which kind removes a 'stop' signal?

column9: The p53 protein is made by a tumor suppressor gene. It stops the cell at a checkpoint when the DNA is damaged. What would a mutation that destroys p53 most likely do?
column14: Make the cell stop dividing forever
column15: Repair all of the cell's DNA damage faster
column16: Let cells with damaged DNA keep dividing
column17: Turn the body cell into a gamete
column28: Without p53, the checkpoint 'brake' is gone, so cells with damaged DNA are not stopped. They keep dividing and pass on the damage, which can lead to cancer. That is why p53 mutations are found in many cancers.
column29: p53 is a brake at a checkpoint. What happens when a brake is removed?

column9: Doctors find a tumor in a patient's breast. Tests also find cancer cells from that tumor in nearby lymph nodes and in the lungs. What does this show?
column14: The tumor is malignant and has metastasized
column15: The tumor is benign and has stayed in place
column16: The tumor cells are going through apoptosis
column17: The patient caught cancer cells from another person
column28: Finding the same cancer cells in the lymph nodes and lungs means cells broke away and spread: metastasis. Only malignant tumors do that. Cancer is not caught from other people.
column29: The cancer cells are now in places far from where the tumor started.

column9: It usually takes several mutations, often over many years, for a normal cell to become a cancer cell. Why?
column14: A cell has several controls, and more than one must fail
column15: The first mutation is usually fixed during the next mitosis
column16: Mutations happen very slowly, about one every ten years
column17: Most single mutations make the cell divide more slowly
column28: Cells have several backup controls: proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, checkpoints, and apoptosis. Usually more than one of them must be broken by mutations before a cell divides out of control, and those mutations build up over years. Mitosis copies mutations instead of fixing them, and while other controls still work they cover for one broken control.
column29: Think of a car with a gas pedal, brakes, and inspection stops. How much has to go wrong to cause a crash?

column9: Which statements describe cancer cells? Select all that apply.
column14: They divide without stopping
column15: They ignore checkpoint signals
column16: They divide by meiosis to make gametes
column17: They avoid apoptosis
column28: Cancer cells divide nonstop, ignore checkpoints, avoid apoptosis, and (when malignant) invade and spread. They divide by mitosis, not meiosis.
column29: Check each statement against what you know about checkpoints, apoptosis, how body cells divide, and malignant tumors.

column9: Skin cancer shows up most often on the face, ears, neck, and arms. What is the best explanation?
column14: Skin cells in those areas have no checkpoints at all
column15: Those areas have fewer cells, so each cell divides more
column16: Those areas get the most UV rays, which damage skin cell DNA
column17: Skin cancer spreads to those areas from the lungs first
column28: The face, ears, neck, and arms are in the sun the most. More UV exposure means more DNA damage and more chances for mutations in cell cycle genes.
column29: Which parts of your body are usually not covered by clothes?

column9: Jae's grandfather smoked for 40 years and then developed lung cancer. Which is the best explanation?
column14: Smoking made his lung cells switch to dividing by meiosis
column15: He breathed in cancer cells that were floating in the smoke
column16: The smoke kept his lung cells from dividing to repair damage
column17: Smoke chemicals caused DNA mutations that built up over years
column28: Carcinogens in tobacco smoke damage DNA. Over 40 years, mutations built up in the genes that control the cell cycle in his lung cells, until some cells divided out of control. Cancer cells are not in the smoke itself.
column29: Think about what smoke does to DNA, and why 40 years might matter.

column9: Radiation can both cause cancer and be used to treat cancer.
column28: True. Radiation damages DNA. Uncontrolled exposure (like too many X-rays or UV rays) can cause mutations that lead to cancer. In radiation therapy, strong doses are aimed right at a tumor to damage the cancer cells' DNA so they can't divide.
column29: Radiation damages DNA. Is that always bad, or does it depend on which cells get hit?

column9: Cells can divide, differentiate, or die. A cell with a broken checkpoint and damaged DNA keeps dividing. Over time, what is most likely to happen?
column14: Its daughter cells fix the damage when they go through meiosis
column15: The damaged cell differentiates into a healthy nerve cell
column16: Daughter cells inherit the damage, add mutations, and form a tumor
column17: The damage is removed after one more round of division
column28: Mitosis copies the damaged DNA into every daughter cell. Without a working checkpoint, more mutations build up with each division, and the growing mass of cells becomes a tumor.
column29: Mitosis makes exact copies. What gets copied along with the DNA?

column9:
Mia looks at the chicken stomach cell data (minutes):
Normal: interphase 540, prophase 60, metaphase 10, anaphase 3, telophase 12
Cancerous: interphase 75, prophase 15, metaphase 2, anaphase 1, telophase 3
She claims, "Cancer cells are dangerous because they spend a bigger share of their cell cycle in mitosis." Which is the best evaluation of her claim?
column14: She is right: more time in mitosis means each division makes extra cells
column15: She is half right: the share is bigger, but the danger is the much shorter cycle
column16: She is wrong: normal cells spend 85 minutes in mitosis, which is far more than 21
column17: She is wrong: both kinds of cells spend about the same share in mitosis
column28: She is right that the share is bigger: mitosis is 21 of 96 minutes (about 22%) for cancer cells but 85 of 625 minutes (about 14%) for normal cells. But a bigger share doesn't make a cell dangerous. The danger is that the whole cancer cycle is much shorter, so cancer cells divide far more often and keep piling up. Normal cells do spend more total minutes in mitosis (85 vs 21), but that compares minutes, not shares. Each mitosis makes two cells no matter how long it takes.
column29: First check her math: what fraction of each cycle is mitosis? Then think about what actually makes a tumor grow fast.

column9: Why is it so important to find cancer early, before it metastasizes?
column14: A tumor that hasn't spread is easier to remove completely
column15: Early cancer cells divide by meiosis, so they are harmless
column16: Spread-out cancer cells turn into benign tumors over time
column17: Early tumors shrink away on their own without treatment
column28: If the cancer is still in one place, surgery (and sometimes radiation) can remove or destroy all of it. Once cells have spread through the blood, tumors may be in many places, which is much harder to treat.
column29: Is it easier to remove one tumor, or tumors in many organs?
